I'm pretty new to the coding/development world. I started off in Python and have made my way into a little bit of C# and PHP. Right now I'm delving head first into Javascript. I'm doing a 1600 hour course at freecodecamp.com. I'm about 100 hours into it, and I can say it's awesome. It totally gets my recommendation.

C# is easy going into, since it is so strictly typed, and it can be used for pretty much anything, if C# seems like a deep end, start with python which is much like C# but easier to start out with, since you don't need to type semi colons and you can easily use pretty much any editor.

Although most concepts are universal, I feel that to some extent different languages tend to teach you different things. I don't think I ever used recursion in Python or Java until I got into Haskell. So while you can start with any language, it might be worth it to eventually contrast it with a different kind of language.

Programming is like playing a musical instrument; At some point you are sufficiently proficient that picking up a new one is not much more than figuring out the fingering. That's not to say you'll become an immediate virtuoso on the new instrument, but for all intents you can get by well enough in fairly short order.

If you're already a coder and you get a job that requires a language that you don't already know then a few weeks with some reference materials will generally be all it takes for you to start being effective.

Truly mastering a language takes years though.

Can anyone ELI5 what this means for the future of Greece and the rest of Europe? If Greece leaves the Eurozone what does this mean for the global economy? How will this effect me, here in the U.S.?

Future for Greece will be to likely leave/get kicked off the Euro. This will be bad in the short term, as their new currency will devalue very quickly, but positive overall. So say if next month they return to the Drachma (their old currency), and the banks offer 1000€ = 1000 Drachma. This will quickly devalue, and probably stabilise in a few months at somewhere like 1000€ = 5000 Drachma.

So that's going to suck if you're a Greek person wanting to travel to or import from Europe. On the other hand, it will be fantastic for Greek exports and tourism, at least once it stabilises. In the long term, it's probably both inevitable and desirable at this stage.

For the Eurozone, it will help it for the time being, but now that a precedent has been set for countries leaving the Euro, it will become more likely for other nations to leave in the future. It will also decrease the odds of any country currently not in the Euro to join up. (For example, Britain was already pretty unlikely to leave the Pound, now it's pretty much guaranteed they won't, at least not for many years). Whether or not the Euro is slowly wound back and countries return to their old currencies is yet to be seen, but there is still a lot of desire in much of the Eurozone to make the single currency work.

In the US, you'll see a short term drop in shares (we've already seen that), but unless Greece completely collapses into anarchy or joins up with Russia and enters into a cold war type stand off with Europe (very unlikely), nothing too drastic is going to happen to the average American or anyone else outside Europe. You might lose 2-3% of your share portfolio's value.
